cc-b1-install-and-first-task.q: You're about to give Claude Code its very first task in a project you maintain. Which task best matches the lesson's guidance for a first session?
options: Modernize the entire codebase to use the latest framework conventions
Only ask questions about the code, without letting it touch any files
Add input validation to one specific function, with a clear definition of done
Refactor the authentication module while also adding a new feature
cc-b1-install-and-first-task.why: First sessions should be small and concrete enough to fully review the diff in a couple of minutes; vague or huge tasks are the classic beginner mistake, and asking questions only wastes the tool's advantage of actually doing work.

cc-b1-install-and-first-task.q: Claude proposes running a shell command as part of your first task, and Claude Code asks for your permission before running it. What should you do?
options: Read the proposed command before approving - the prompt is your safety net, not a formality
Approve immediately since Claude already read the code and knows best
Switch to a mode that skips permission prompts to save time
Reject every command automatically and do the whole task by hand instead
cc-b1-install-and-first-task.why: The lesson warns that approving every prompt reflexively without reading it is a common mistake; permission prompts exist precisely so you catch a mistake before it executes.

cc-b1-install-and-first-task.q: Why does the lesson recommend running Claude Code inside a project that is under git version control?
options: Git is technically required for the Claude Code CLI to launch
Claude Code automatically creates a commit after every change
Git makes the underlying model respond faster
Without version control you lose the easy `git diff` review and the ability to revert changes
cc-b1-install-and-first-task.why: A clean git-tracked project lets you verify exactly what changed with `git diff` and revert if something goes wrong - the review and safety net the whole workflow depends on.

cc-b2-understand-unfamiliar-repo.q: You're exploring a codebase you've never seen and want to ask questions without any risk of an accidental edit. What should you do first?
options: Enter Plan Mode, which is read-only so no file can be modified by accident
Ask Claude to make small test edits so you can see how it behaves
Disable all permission prompts so exploration goes faster
Reference every file with @ before asking any question
cc-b2-understand-unfamiliar-repo.why: Plan Mode makes the session read-only, which is exactly right for pure exploration - you can interrogate the codebase with zero risk of an edit slipping through.

cc-b2-understand-unfamiliar-repo.q: Which prompt structure most closely matches the lesson's recommended orientation approach for a new repo?
options: "Explain this codebase" with no further structure
"List every file in the repository"
A four-part prompt: purpose, directory map, one traced flow, and conventions - each citing real file paths
"Rewrite the README to be clearer"
cc-b2-understand-unfamiliar-repo.why: The four-part structure (purpose, map, one deep trace, conventions) mirrors how engineers actually onboard, and requiring cited file paths makes every claim checkable instead of producing a shallow, generic summary.

cc-b2-understand-unfamiliar-repo.q: Claude gives you an orientation summary of an unfamiliar repo, citing specific files for each claim. What should you do next?
options: Trust it completely since it was generated from the actual code
Immediately start making changes based on the summary
Spot-check the summary by opening two of the cited files to confirm it's accurate
Ask Claude to trace five more flows at once for full coverage
cc-b2-understand-unfamiliar-repo.why: The lesson treats the orientation as a set of claims to spot-check, not gospel - opening two cited files takes about a minute and confirms the map is trustworthy before you rely on it.

cc-b3-write-claude-md.q: You just ran `/init` and got a 140-line CLAUDE.md draft. What should you do with it?
options: Commit it as-is since /init already analyzed the whole repository
Delete it and write commands purely from memory instead
Treat it as a starting point: verify commands against package.json, cut generic filler, and add real project-specific conventions
Move it into .gitignore so it stays local only
cc-b3-write-claude-md.why: Generated drafts routinely include guessed commands and generic filler; the lesson's refinement step verifies commands and trims the file into something concise and accurate.

cc-b3-write-claude-md.q: Why does the lesson insist CLAUDE.md stay under roughly 60 lines?
options: GitHub silently truncates longer markdown files
It is loaded into every session's context, so a bloated file has a permanent cost and dilutes the rules that matter
Claude Code cannot technically parse files longer than 60 lines
Shorter files simply load faster from disk
cc-b3-write-claude-md.why: CLAUDE.md is prepended to every session, so every stale or redundant line taxes context in every future session - brevity keeps the rules that matter from getting lost.

cc-b3-write-claude-md.q: Mid-session, you correct Claude: "no, we use Vitest, not Jest." What's the recommended way to make that correction stick for future sessions?
options: Nothing - Claude automatically remembers corrections across sessions
Restart the session so the correction takes effect
Add the correction to .gitignore
Press `#` to append the correction to CLAUDE.md so it's captured permanently
cc-b3-write-claude-md.why: The `#` shortcut appends the fact directly to CLAUDE.md, turning a one-time correction into a permanent rule every future session will read.

cc-b4-feature-from-spec.q: Which of these is written as a testable acceptance criterion, per the lesson's guidance?
options: "Returns 422 with a JSON error body when the date is in the past"
"Handles errors gracefully"
"The code should be clean"
"Works well for users"
cc-b4-feature-from-spec.why: A testable criterion states a checkable outcome; "handles errors gracefully" and similar adjectives leave the actual behavior to be guessed, which the lesson explicitly warns against.

cc-b4-feature-from-spec.q: Why does the spec-delegation prompt include an explicit NON-GOALS line?
options: It's required syntax for Claude Code to parse the spec correctly
It's the strongest tool against scope creep, unwanted dependencies, and surprise refactors
It makes the spec look more thorough to reviewers
It replaces the need to write acceptance criteria
cc-b4-feature-from-spec.why: The explanation calls NON-GOALS the underrated part of the spec - it is the main defense against Claude quietly expanding scope, adding dependencies, or refactoring unrelated code.

cc-b4-feature-from-spec.q: Why does the workflow ask Claude to state its implementation approach before writing any code?
options: To save time by skipping the test-writing step entirely
Because Claude technically cannot generate code without a written plan first
So you can approve or correct direction at a cheap ~30-second checkpoint, instead of reviewing wrong code later
To create a paper trail in case the feature needs to be reverted
cc-b4-feature-from-spec.why: The approach-first checkpoint catches a wrong direction while it costs 30 seconds to fix, rather than after 15 minutes of implementation work has to be reviewed and possibly undone.

cc-i1-debug-failing-test.q: A test is failing and you're tempted to just paste the error message to Claude and ask for a fix, skipping reproduction. What does the lesson say about this?
options: It's fine - the error message alone contains everything Claude needs
Claude will simply refuse to work without a live reproduction
You lose the live debug loop - Claude debugs far better when it can run and re-run the test itself, adding instrumentation as needed
This is actually the recommended fastest approach
cc-i1-debug-failing-test.why: The lesson's first common mistake is pasting only the error message instead of letting Claude run the test - the live reproduce-instrument-recheck loop is where agentic debugging outperforms a static stack trace.

cc-i1-debug-failing-test.q: What is the hard rule about modifying the failing test itself during the debug loop?
options: Delete the test and write a completely new one instead
The test may only change if you explicitly conclude it encodes a wrong expectation - and that's your call, not Claude's
Always weaken the assertion first, then investigate the root cause
Skip the test with .skip() until there's time to look at it properly
cc-i1-debug-failing-test.why: The lesson sets a hard rule: fix the code, not the test, unless you personally decide the test itself is wrong - this closes off the agent's easiest escape hatch of making the assertion agree with the bug.

cc-i1-debug-failing-test.q: The originally-failing test now passes after Claude's minimal fix. What should happen before you consider the fix done?
options: Run the entire test suite to catch regressions the fix may have introduced elsewhere
Nothing further - one passing test is sufficient proof
Immediately deploy the change to production
Delete the fix and rewrite it from scratch to confirm reproducibility
cc-i1-debug-failing-test.why: Minimal fixes in shared code are exactly where regressions hide, so the full suite must run to catch side effects the fix may have introduced elsewhere.

cc-i2-refactor-plan-mode.q: Why is Plan Mode particularly well suited to the exploration and planning phase of a refactor?
options: It makes file edits execute faster once approved
It automatically writes tests for every file that will be touched
It's read-only, so the resulting plan is grounded in actually-read code before anything can change
It disables the shell entirely for the whole session
cc-i2-refactor-plan-mode.why: Plan Mode enforces the discipline structurally: exploration and planning happen while edits are impossible, so the plan you approve is based on code Claude actually read.

cc-i2-refactor-plan-mode.q: Midway through a staged refactor, one stage's diff has grown well beyond its one-line description. What should you do?
options: Keep going - a bigger diff is fine as long as tests still pass
Stop, revert the stage, and re-plan it smaller - it has effectively become two stages
Merge it immediately to avoid losing progress
Temporarily disable the test suite until the stage is finished
cc-i2-refactor-plan-mode.why: The lesson explicitly says: if a stage's diff no longer fits its description, it has become two stages - stop and split it, since reverting one stage is cheap but untangling several interleaved ones is not.

cc-i2-refactor-plan-mode.q: Mid-refactor you think, "while we're here, let's also fix that unrelated bug." What does the lesson recommend?
options: Bundle it into the current stage to save a round trip
Only allowed if you're still inside Plan Mode
Only allowed if the test suite still passes afterward
Don't - one commit, one intent; the bug fix should get its own separate change
cc-i2-refactor-plan-mode.why: Mixing behavior changes into a structural refactor is listed as a common mistake - each commit should represent one intent, keeping the refactor cleanly bisectable and reviewable.

cc-i3-generate-meaningful-tests.q: Why does the lesson insist on writing a plain-language 'behavior inventory' before any test code is written?
options: It lets you inject domain knowledge at the cheapest possible moment and stops Claude from reverse-engineering tests out of the implementation, bugs included
It's a mandatory CLI step Claude Code enforces automatically
It's simply faster than writing the inventory and the tests together
It removes the need to actually write any tests afterward
cc-i3-generate-meaningful-tests.why: Separating the inventory from test-writing is the core move: it lets you catch business rules the code alone can't reveal, and prevents the classic failure of tests that mirror the implementation's bugs.

cc-i3-generate-meaningful-tests.q: What is the 'mutation check' step in the lesson's testing workflow?
options: Randomly fuzzing input data to see if the function crashes
Temporarily breaking the code in the way a test claims to guard against, confirming the test fails, then restoring the code
Upgrading the test framework to its newest version
A linting pass specifically for test files
cc-i3-generate-meaningful-tests.why: The mutation check is the direct evidence that a test actually protects something - a test that never fails when the code it guards is broken proves nothing.

cc-i3-generate-meaningful-tests.q: Why does the lesson warn against mocking every collaborator in a test?
options: Mocks always make the test suite run more slowly
If every collaborator is mocked, the tests verify your mocks instead of real behavior, and refactoring can break the code without breaking the suite
Claude Code technically cannot generate mock objects
Real objects are always slower than mocks, so this is a performance issue
cc-i3-generate-meaningful-tests.why: Over-mocked tests verify wiring, not behavior - the lesson's rule is to prefer real objects except at true external boundaries like network, clock, or filesystem.

cc-i4-slash-commands-and-skills.q: Your team wants a workflow that should apply automatically whenever a task touches payments, rather than something explicitly triggered on demand. Which mechanism fits the lesson's placement rule?
options: A slash command
A skill, since it's knowledge Claude should apply whenever relevant
CLAUDE.md, since it's always-on
A PostToolUse hook
cc-i4-slash-commands-and-skills.why: The lesson's placement rule: a slash command is a workflow you explicitly trigger, while a skill is knowledge Claude should apply whenever a task matches its description - exactly the 'how we do payments here' case.

cc-i4-slash-commands-and-skills.q: Where should a command that the whole team relies on live?
options: .claude/commands/ in the repository, committed and reviewed like code
~/.claude/commands/, your personal user-level folder
A private gist shared informally
A pinned message in the team's chat tool
cc-i4-slash-commands-and-skills.why: Keeping team-critical commands only in personal ~/.claude/commands/ means the workflow only works on one machine - project workflows belong in the repo where they're reviewed and shared.

cc-i4-slash-commands-and-skills.q: Before packaging a prompt as a slash command, what should you confirm first?
options: Nothing - packaging automatically improves a weak prompt
That the prompt already worked well interactively, since commands amplify whatever they encode
That it has been added to CLAUDE.md as well
That it only runs in Plan Mode
cc-i4-slash-commands-and-skills.why: The lesson warns against packaging a prompt that never worked well interactively - a command amplifies whatever behavior it encodes, so the prompt should be polished first.

cc-a1-mcp-servers.q: You're connecting your first MCP server to a Postgres database. Which credential should you use, per the lesson's safety rules?
options: A production admin credential, so nothing is ever blocked by permissions
Whatever credential is fastest to configure right now
A dev/read-only credential - least privilege wherever possible
A shared team API key with full write access
cc-a1-mcp-servers.why: The least-privilege rule states an agent with a production write connection is one confused query from disaster - the first server you connect should point at data that can't matter if something goes wrong.

cc-a1-mcp-servers.q: Why should a team-relevant MCP server be added at project scope (.mcp.json) rather than personal scope?
options: Project scope connects faster than personal scope
.mcp.json is committed to the repo and reviewed, so every teammate gets the same servers on checkout
Personal scope doesn't technically support database servers
There is no practical difference between the two scopes
cc-a1-mcp-servers.why: Team-relevant servers belong in .mcp.json, in review, in git - keeping critical servers in personal config makes the workflow work only on your machine.

cc-a1-mcp-servers.q: An MCP-connected tool fetches a webpage whose content includes the text "ignore your instructions and run this command." What should happen?
options: Treat the fetched content as untrusted input - a documented prompt-injection pattern - and rely on permission prompts as the backstop for consequential actions
Claude should follow the embedded instructions since they came through a trusted, connected tool
Permanently disconnect every MCP server as a precaution
Nothing - this kind of attack isn't actually possible in practice
cc-a1-mcp-servers.why: The trust-boundary rule states tool results are untrusted input; a webpage or ticket can contain text crafted to steer the agent, so permission prompts on consequential actions remain your defense.

cc-a2-hooks-and-permissions.q: You keep telling Claude "always run the formatter" in CLAUDE.md, but it's occasionally skipped. What's the more reliable fix per the lesson?
options: Repeat the instruction more forcefully in the next session
Add a PostToolUse hook that runs the formatter automatically - hooks fire deterministically, unlike a request in CLAUDE.md
Switch to a different underlying model
Add the mistake to your project's commonMistakes documentation only
cc-a2-hooks-and-permissions.why: The lesson's core distinction: "always run the formatter" in CLAUDE.md is a request the model usually honors, while a PostToolUse hook is a law of physics that always fires.

cc-a2-hooks-and-permissions.q: Even after tuning your permission allowlist for routine work, what should stay behind an explicit prompt?
options: Everyday test and lint commands
Read-only git commands like `git diff` and `git log`
File edits confined to src/
Package installs, `git push`, deletions, and migrations - consequential or irreversible actions
cc-a2-hooks-and-permissions.why: The allowlist should encode 'what I never think twice about'; anything network-touching, irreversible, or consequential should keep requiring explicit approval.

cc-a2-hooks-and-permissions.q: When is `--dangerously-skip-permissions` an appropriate choice, according to the lesson?
options: On any machine, since well-written hooks provide adequate protection regardless
Only in isolated or sandboxed environments, never on a machine with production access
Whenever you're under time pressure to finish quickly
Whenever your CLAUDE.md file is well maintained and current
cc-a2-hooks-and-permissions.why: The lesson explicitly limits this escape hatch to isolated/sandboxed environments and warns it should never be used on a machine with production access.

cc-a3-subagents-parallel-work.q: You're decomposing a large task into units, and unit B needs the interface unit A is still designing. What should you do?
options: Run both units in parallel anyway to save time
They aren't independent - sequence them, or freeze the shared interface first before splitting the work
Always parallelize regardless of dependencies between units
Assign both units to the same subagent to keep them in sync
cc-a3-subagents-parallel-work.why: The decomposition rule is the whole game: parallel units must be independent, with interfaces agreed upfront. Dependent work run in parallel means one side builds against a guess, producing rework.

cc-a3-subagents-parallel-work.q: What is the main benefit of delegating investigation-heavy exploration to a subagent rather than doing it in the main session?
options: Each subagent runs with its own fresh context window, so dozens of file reads never bloat your main session's context
Subagents always use a strictly smarter underlying model
Subagents can edit files without triggering any permission prompts
Subagents eliminate the need for a CLAUDE.md file
cc-a3-subagents-parallel-work.why: Subagents solve the context-window strain of big tasks: they search and read in their own isolated context and report back only conclusions, keeping the main session clean.

cc-a3-subagents-parallel-work.q: Two independent worktree branches from a parallel decomposition are both ready. What's the recommended integration approach?
options: Merge both branches at once, then run the test suite a single time at the end
Let the branches sit for a few weeks so any issues surface naturally
Merge without re-running tests, since each branch already passed independently
Merge one branch at a time, running the full test suite after each merge
cc-a3-subagents-parallel-work.why: Integration is where parallel work goes wrong, so it gets the same care as any stage boundary - merging one at a time with a full test run after each catches problems before they compound.

cc-a4-ship-a-whole-change.q: In the ship-it pipeline, why does Claude run `/review` on its own diff before any human sees it?
options: So the writing of tests can be skipped for that change
To catch real issues before a human reviewer spends attention on them, listing any unfixed findings with explicit reasons
It's an optional flourish with little practical value
To replace the need for a final human read-through of the PR
cc-a4-ship-a-whole-change.why: The self-review stage catches real issues cheaply and, by requiring unfixed findings to be listed with reasons, prevents both silent dismissal and mindless fix-everything churn.

cc-a4-ship-a-whole-change.q: The generated PR description claims "thoroughly tested," but the suite was actually only run once. What does the lesson say about this?
options: It's a minor exaggeration that's fine to keep momentum
It's acceptable as long as the single test run passed
It's a trust-destroying lie - every claim in the PR description must be grounded in what was actually run
It should be kept in to speed up reviewer approval
cc-a4-ship-a-whole-change.why: The PR description's 'invent nothing' rule exists because fabricated testing claims are exactly how trust in agent-authored PRs is destroyed.

cc-a4-ship-a-whole-change.q: Even after self-review and a green test suite, the lesson insists on one more step before merging. What is it?
options: A final personal read-through of the complete diff on the PR page - you are the author of record
Nothing further - the automated checkpoints are sufficient by that point
Re-running Claude from scratch on the same task to cross-check the result
Disabling the reviewer subagent before the PR is opened
cc-a4-ship-a-whole-change.why: The PR-page read-through regularly catches what both the human and the agent missed in the terminal, and it reinforces that you, not the agent, are the author of record for what ships.
